purpose: Droxidopa is used to treat dizziness, lightheadedness, and fainting that happens when you stand up, a condition called neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (NOH). This problem occurs in people with certain nervous system disorders like Parkinson's disease or other conditions that affect how your body controls blood pressure. It helps your blood pressure stay stable when you change positions so you feel less dizzy and more steady on your feet.
how_it_works: Your body normally releases a chemical called norepinephrine to help keep your blood pressure up when you stand. In some people, the nervous system does not make enough of this chemical, causing blood pressure to drop when they stand up. Droxidopa is converted in your body into norepinephrine, helping replace what is missing and keeping your blood pressure at a safer level when you move around.
common_side_effects: Headache, dizziness, nausea, high blood pressure (especially when lying down), tiredness, and swelling in the hands or feet are the most common side effects. Let your doctor know if any of these bother you.
warnings: This medication can raise your blood pressure too high when you are lying flat, which can be dangerous and increase the risk of stroke or heart problems. You should sleep with your head and upper body raised and avoid lying flat. Tell your doctor right away if you have a severe headache, vision changes, or chest pain. It should be used carefully if you have heart disease, kidney problems, or if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 100 mg taken by mouth three times a day — in the morning, at midday, and in the late afternoon. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose every 24 to 48 hours as needed, up to a maximum of 600 mg three times a day. Do not take it within 3 to 4 hours of bedtime to avoid dangerously high blood pressure while you sleep.
